title: The Impossible Document

narrative.text: The corridor outside the Great Hall is narrow — intentionally so, built in an era when architects believed that transitions between spaces should feel like transitions. Aldric Theron is explaining something with his hands — the precise, rhythmic gestures of someone who has been making the same argument for weeks and is refining it rather than abandoning it. Dražen Kolvar is listening. That is the unsettling part. He is not disagreeing exactly. He is asking questions that are not quite questions.
And you believe that's workable.
I believe it's right.
Those aren't the same thing.
No. But one usually follows the other if you're patient.

Kolvar looks like he does not believe that. He notices you approaching. His expression shifts — not to hostility, but to the particular awareness of a man who wants to continue an argument but recognizes that a new audience has arrived.
Chancellor, perhaps you can explain to Aldric that constitutional conventions require more than optimism.

The Great Hall of Parliament has not been used for a legislative session of this scale since 1934 — since the last parliament before Halvek dissolved it. Someone has made a point of noting this in the official program. Professor Theron, probably. He is the sort of man who understands that architecture and precedent do the same work.

All one hundred and twelve sitting members of parliament have gathered. The gallery above is packed — journalists with notebooks, citizens who queued since dawn, a row of foreign observers in diplomatic grey. The Arcturian and Orythian ambassadors are both present, seated on opposite sides of the gallery, pointedly ignoring each other. Whatever happens in this room today will be translated into cables and sent to capitals that care about the result for reasons entirely unrelated to Veltrian democracy.

Theron approaches the podium with the careful deliberateness of a man who has spent thirty years preparing for this particular moment and does not intend to waste it on haste. He sets his document — ninety-four pages, distributed this morning to every MP — on the lectern and looks out at the assembled chamber with an expression you recognize: the specific satisfaction of someone who believes that ideas, properly arranged, are more powerful than armies.

In 1897, the founders of this Republic wrote a constitution in forty-eight hours of revolutionary excitement, on the belief that the words would create the reality. They were correct. The words created a reality — and then, in 1934, a general with a better army decided that his words would create a different reality. We are here today because we have learned something those founders had not yet learned: a constitution is only as strong as the institutions built to defend it, and institutions are only as strong as the citizens who insist upon them.

The document before you does not ask you to be idealists. It asks you to be architects. We are not writing poetry. We are building the load-bearing walls of a state that will outlast every person in this room.

He proceeds through the provisions methodically: the independent judiciary, the bill of rights, the term limits, the dissolution of the BNI, the workers' right to strike, the Dravenni language provisions, the separation of church and state, the land reform clause. Each one is presented with historical context, comparative examples, and a patient explanation of why the Halvek constitution failed in this specific dimension. It is a masterwork of academic exposition. It is also, you can see from the expressions in the chamber, a declaration of war on at least four of the seven factions represented in this room.
Dražen Kolvar is on his feet before Theron has finished his last sentence.

The Professor speaks of architects. Very well. Let us examine what he has designed. A judiciary appointed by a commission that this government controls. Emergency powers neutered at the precise moment when Tyvaren conducts military exercises twelve kilometers from our northern border. An intelligence service constitutionally dissolved — constitutionally, so that no future government can rebuild it — at the same moment our eastern neighbor is a failed state hemorrhaging armed militias. The Professor has designed a beautiful building with no foundation and no walls. He has designed, with great elegance, a ruin.

The Halvek constitution was imperfect. I have never claimed otherwise. But imperfect institutions are still institutions. What the Chancellor's professor has written is not a reform. It is a demolition. And when you demolish the only load-bearing wall in a building, Chancellor — regardless of the reason — the ceiling falls on everyone inside.

He is not entirely wrong. That is the infuriating thing about Kolvar. He is never entirely wrong. He locates the one real flaw in every argument and stands inside it until it feels like the whole structure.

Theron catches your eye from the podium. He has heard Kolvar's attack — the elegant ruin, the demolition, the ceiling falling on everyone inside. His philosophical counter-argument is visible in his expression, forming, ready to be delivered with the same patient precision he has brought to every exchange today. But instead he steps down from the lectern and walks directly to you. He does not speak loudly. This is not for the gallery.
Remove Kolvar from the drafting committee. Today. Before the afternoon session.

The room around you goes quiet. This is not the Theron anyone expected — not the academic quoting 1897, not the philosopher building cathedrals of principle. This is something else. Clean. Cold. Surgical.
Because he has been talking to Vael's people.

He produces a folder — not from his lectern, but from inside his jacket, where it has been waiting. He places it on the table in front of you. Opens it. Four letters. Vael Group letterhead. Dates spanning the last two weeks. Meeting locations. Topics discussed: the judiciary clause, the land reform provision, the dissolution of the BNI. All the provisions Kolvar just attacked. All the ones Vael wants removed.

I have the letters. Every one. He does not know I have them. Remove him this afternoon and we can still pass the draft before the end of the session. Wait until tomorrow and he will have time to organize. That is the calculation. There is no philosophy in this one, Chancellor. There is only the question of whether we act now or we lose the constitution.
He returns to his notes. The moment passes as if it never happened. The philosopher has become the tactician, and it took only the time it takes to open a folder.

Soraya Khaled does not wait to be recognized. She stands from the Workers' Unity benches and her voice fills the chamber without effort — the voice of a woman who spent eight years being told her words were illegal, who has not stopped speaking since.

I've read every page of this document twice since five this morning. I want to tell Professor Theron something. It is an extraordinary piece of work. It protects rights I did not expect this government to protect, and for that I am genuinely grateful. But I want to tell the Chancellor something different. This document does not protect my people from poverty. It protects them from arbitrary arrest — which matters, it matters enormously — but it does not tell the miners of Kravenstal how they will eat next winter.

There is one land reform clause. One workers' strike right. Two provisions in ninety-four pages that address the material conditions of sixty percent of the population of Veltria. The rest is beautifully written procedure for how the people who already have power will distribute it among themselves more fairly. I will vote for this document because the alternative is the Halvek constitution. But I want the Chancellor to understand what she is asking me to accept when she calls this a beginning rather than an arrival.

The hall absorbs both speeches. Journalists are writing furiously. In the gallery, you catch the face of the Arcturian ambassador, Harrison Cole, watching the proceedings with what could be satisfaction or concern — it is difficult to tell with him, which you suspect is intentional.
They've both fired their opening positions. Kolvar has thirty-eight votes. Khaled has nineteen. You need fifty-seven to pass a constitutional referendum. The math is what it is.
The math is always what it is. Vyktor has a talent for expressing the entire problem in the smallest number of words. You sometimes wonder if that is a gift or a refusal to engage with complexity.

The gallery is watching. The chamber is watching. This is the moment when the convention's tone is set — not in the weeks of committee work that will follow, but in this room, in the next sixty seconds, in whatever you choose to say or not say. Every journalist in the press gallery has their pen ready. Whatever you do now will be the headline.

monologue: Theron believes in the constitution like it is a living thing. Kolvar sees it as a surrender document. Both are in this room. Both are waiting for me to pick a side — and I still do not know which side is correct.

choices.text: "The Professor's draft is the draft. We will discuss its implementation, not its surrender. I did not win an election on a mandate to pass a version of the Halvek constitution with better typography."

reactions.text: Thirty-eight votes just went into opposition. Kolvar's bloc is now formally against the draft. You have drawn the line. Now you have to hold it.
Theron nods once — the smallest nod possible, the kind that contains more relief than he would ever put into words. He returns to his notes and does not look at you again. He does not need to.
Kolvar says nothing. He writes a single word on the notepad in front of him — you cannot see what it is — and closes it. The silence is more worrying than any of his arguments were.

choices.text: "The convention is a process, not a verdict. Every faction will have the opportunity to argue its case through the proper channels. That is what democratic deliberation looks like — it is slower and louder than a decree, and it is better for both of those reasons."

reactions.text: That buys us two weeks of process. Use them.
Chancellor, I will hold you to this. The workers of Kravenstal will hold you to this. Process is a promise — and promises have to be kept.

Theron removes his glasses and cleans them with the edge of his sleeve — a gesture you have learned means he is disappointed but understands the political logic. He does not argue. That is itself an argument.

choices.text: "This document belongs to the people of Veltria — not to the members of this chamber. I am opening the text for public comment. Every citizen may write to the convention. We will hold public meetings in all six provinces. The parliamentarians in this room will answer to their constituents, not to each other."

reactions.text: That will make the process louder and longer. Also harder to control. Also possibly more democratic. I am not objecting. I am noting.
She nods — not quite smiling but not quite not. You have just given the people a door into this process. The Halvekist bloc will spend the next three weeks trying to close it.
Kolvar rises without asking for recognition. He walks to the exit slowly, past three rows of journalists who write down the fact that he left. The exit itself is a statement.

choices.text: Make no statement. Let the chamber debate. Observe.

reactions.text: Vyktor looks at you for a full three seconds. He says nothing. The silence is not agreement — it is the particular quiet of someone who has already calculated the political cost of your decision and is choosing not to name it out loud.

Theron catches your eye from across the chamber. He had expected something. You can see him adjust his expectations in real time — the philosopher's version of pain. He does not speak for the remainder of the session.

Soraya Khaled looks at the gallery, then at you, then back at the gallery. She does not speak again for the remainder of the session. The absence of her voice is louder than the speech she did not give.
